readerTitle: New Coke: the move that let Pepsi write the headline
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Coca-Cola, PepsiCo, 1975~1985 콜라 전쟁) + 가상 적용 (배관 업체, 사무실 IT 지원 업체)
insight: 경쟁 상황에서 내 수의 결과는 고객 반응만으로 정해지지 않는다. 경쟁자가 그 수에 어떻게 답할지, 그리고 그 수가 무엇을 인정하는 신호가 되는지까지 계산해야 한다.
misconception: 고객 테스트에서 이기는 선택이면 경쟁에서도 이긴다. 경쟁자가 정한 기준에서 이기면 경쟁자를 이긴 것이다.

sources.text: The Coca-Cola Company, "The Real Story of New Coke" (회사 공식 역사 자료: 1985년 4월 23일 발표, 1985년 7월 11일 Coca-Cola Classic 복귀, 약 20만 건의 맛 테스트, 고객 항의)
Enrico, R. & Kornbluth, J. (1986). The Other Guy Blinked: How Pepsi Won the Cola Wars. (Pepsi의 신문 광고와 대응)
PepsiCo, company history (1975년 Pepsi Challenge 시작)
Gladwell, M. (2005). Blink. (한 모금 테스트가 더 단 음료에 유리하다는 주장)

factChecks.note: 발표일 1985년 4월 23일, Classic 복귀 발표 1985년 7월 11일(79일)은 Coca-Cola 공식 자료로 게시 전 다시 확인하세요.
"about 200,000 taste tests"는 Coca-Cola 공식 자료의 수치입니다. 자료마다 19만~20만으로 조금씩 다르므로 "about"으로 적었습니다.
Pepsi가 신문 전면 광고로 "the other guy blinked"라고 선언했다는 내용은 Enrico(1986)와 다수 언론에 나옵니다. 직원에게 하루 휴가를 줬다는 이야기는 출처마다 표현이 달라 카드에 "reportedly"로 표시했습니다.
Donald Keough의 "not that dumb, not that smart" 발언(1985년 7월 Classic 복귀 기자회견)은 원문 문장을 그대로 인용하지 않고 요약해 적었습니다. 게시 전 원문을 확인하세요.
Pepsi Challenge 시작 연도(1975년, 텍사스 댈러스)는 PepsiCo 자료로 확인하세요. 당시 시장점유율 수치는 출처마다 기준이 달라 카드에 쓰지 않고 "lead was shrinking"으로만 적었습니다.

cards.title: New Coke: the move that let Pepsi write the headline
body: In April 1985, Coca-Cola replaced the recipe it had sold for 99 years. It had tested the new taste on about 200,000 people, and most liked it better.
Seventy-nine days later, the old recipe was back on shelves. The taste tests weren't wrong. The company had studied its customers closely. It hadn't studied its rival's next move.

image.label: Two cola cans facing each other like chess pieces
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 체스판 위에 빨간 캔과 파란 캔이 마주 서 있고, 빨간 캔이 한 칸 움직인 순간 파란 캔 쪽에서 말풍선이 올라옴. 실제 로고, 글자, 상표 도안은 절대 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Your rival keeps winning blind taste tests.
body: Since 1975, Pepsi has run the *Pepsi Challenge*: shoppers sip two unlabeled colas and most pick Pepsi. Your lead in the market has been shrinking for years.
Your own blind tests find a sweeter new recipe that beats both Pepsi and your current Coke. What do you do?

options.text: Replace the old recipe with the new one
options.feedback: You win the taste test Pepsi built. But you also tell the world Pepsi was right, and you take away something loyal customers loved.

options.text: Launch the new recipe as a second cola and keep the original
options.feedback: Safer for loyal drinkers, and you test the taste for real. You still accept Pepsi's claim that sip tests decide the contest.

options.text: Keep the recipe and compete on what a sip test can't measure
options.feedback: You give up a possible taste win, but you refuse to play on the board your rival chose. Pepsi gets nothing new to brag about.

cards.title: Coca-Cola chose A. Pepsi was ready.
body: Coca-Cola announced New Coke on April 23, 1985. Pepsi answered with newspaper ads saying, in effect, that *the other guy blinked*. It reportedly gave its staff a day off to celebrate.
Then loyal Coke drinkers revolted. The company was flooded with angry calls and letters. On July 11, it brought back the original as **Coca-Cola Classic**.

image.label: Timeline from April 23 to July 11, 1985
image.brief: 가로 타임라인 인포그래픽. "Apr 23: new recipe", "Rival: 'They blinked'", "Calls and letters pile up", "Jul 11: Classic returns". 중간에 쌓이는 편지 더미 일러스트. 로고 없음.

cards.title: Your move includes your rival's reply
body: In a game, the payoff of your move depends on your rival's **best response**: the reply that helps them most.
Coca-Cola asked, "Will customers like this taste?" It needed a second question: "What is the best thing Pepsi can say the day we do this?" The answer was easy. *They changed because we won.*
A new recipe that tested well became, in public, an admission of defeat.

cards.title: Pepsi had already chosen the board.
body: The Pepsi Challenge made one sip of an unlabeled drink the yardstick. Critics, including Malcolm Gladwell in *Blink*, later argued that sip tests favor sweeter drinks. Drinking a whole can at home, with the label showing, is a different test.
By changing its taste to win sips, Coca-Cola agreed that sips were what mattered. Its move was also a **signal**, and the signal said Pepsi's yardstick was the right one.

cards.title: The same trap shows up in small rivalries.
body: A rival plumbing company runs ads: "Flat prices. No surprise bills." You charge by the hour, and most of your customers come back because your plumbers explain the work clearly.
If you suddenly switch to flat prices, your rival can say, "Even they admit hourly billing was a rip-off." You've adopted their idea and handed them the credit.

image.label: Two vans, one copying the other's sign
image.brief: 동네 거리의 배관 업체 밴 두 대. 한 대 옆면에 "Flat prices" 문구, 다른 한 대가 같은 문구를 새로 붙이는 중이고 첫 번째 밴 운전자가 웃고 있음. 실제 업체명과 로고 없음.

cards.softwareNote: When a rival's launch post says "the only tool with X," rushing out X with a big announcement can confirm their story. Ask what their best reply to your launch will be before you ship it loudly.

cards.title: Hindsight makes this look easier than it was.
body: Doing nothing has costs too. Coca-Cola's lead really was shrinking, and sometimes a rival is right and you should change.
The lesson isn't "never respond." Respond after you've played out the rival's reply and decided you can live with it.

Some people still claim New Coke was a planned stunt. Coca-Cola's president, Donald Keough, answered that the company was neither that dumb nor that smart. Coca-Cola stayed the market leader, but nobody planned it that way.

cards.title: Now it's office IT support.
body: You provide IT support to small offices. A rival's ads say: "We answer in 15 minutes. Others take a day." Your clients mostly stay because one account manager knows their setup.
What's your move?

options.text: Launch a campaign promising a 10-minute response
options.feedback: You may win the speed claim, but you've agreed speed is the contest. The rival can reply "they're copying us," and you've raised your costs.

options.text: Quietly speed up urgent cases; keep marketing your account managers
options.feedback: You fix a real weakness without signaling defeat. The rival's best reply gets weaker, and the contest stays on ground you win.
You avoid giving the rival a headline. But if some clients truly need fast help, you lose them without a fight.

cards.title: Before you move, write your rival's headline.
body: A move against a rival is judged twice: by customers, and by the rival who gets to say what it means.
**Try it today:** pick a change you're planning in response to a competitor. Write the one sentence they'd most like to say about it. If it hurts, change the move or how you make it.
